title: the standing prayer
hook: the standing prayer; "sarbat da bhala" — the good of all

segments.voice: Yesterday: the Panj Pyare, five strangers, one family. Today, the prayer that remembers them every time it's said.

End of the service. Someone steps forward, and the whole room rises: palms together, facing the scripture. Plenty of people have stood for it since they were small without knowing what's being said. Then a voice calls out, bole so nihal, and the room shouts back, sat sri akal. Today, what everyone is standing for.
screen: `THE ROOM RISES.` → `PALMS TOGETHER.` → `WHAT IS BEING SAID?`

segments.voice: It's the Ardas. The word comes from Persian, for a petition, a humble request. Sikhs say it standing, facing the Guru Granth Sahib, at the end of services and before anything important: a wedding, a journey, a new home. It has a shape. It opens by remembering the Gurus, one by one, from Nanak on. Then it remembers more: the scripture, the five beloved from yesterday, and the men and women who suffered for their faith. A prayer with a long memory. Then it turns personal. The one leading adds the day's requests: a new baby, a grandmother in the hospital, thanks for a new job. So no two are quite the same. And the end never changes. It asks for chardi kala, ever-rising spirits, and then three words: sarbat da bhala. The good of all. Not the good of Sikhs, or of this room. Everyone. After all that memory, the last thing asked for is the well-being of the whole world. Then comes the shout. Bole so nihal: whoever says it is blessed. And the answer, sat sri akal: true is the timeless one. The same words many Sikhs use to say hello.
screen: `ARDAS — A HUMBLE REQUEST.` · `A PRAYER WITH A LONG MEMORY.` · `THE DAY'S OWN REQUESTS.` · `SARBAT DA BHALA — THE GOOD OF ALL.`

segments.voice: Three breaths with the bell. Stand if you can, palms together. On the first, bring to mind the people closest to you. On the second, widen it to strangers. On the third, widen it once more, to someone you find hard to wish well.
Ardas. The standing prayer: it remembers, it asks, and it ends by asking for the good of all. Fifth word.
Your line: for everyone, not just us. Those are the prayer's last words, and they leave nobody out. Day five, done.

howItsDone: Sikhs stand with palms joined, facing the Guru Granth Sahib, while one person leads the Ardas at the end of services and before important events; it closes by asking for chardi kala and sarbat da bhala, the good of all, and the congregation answers the call "bole so nihal" with "sat sri akal."

what it means: the standing prayer: it remembers the Gurus and the martyrs, carries the day's requests, and ends with the good of all.

what a scholar hears: the Ardas isn't in the Guru Granth Sahib. its opening comes from Guru Gobind Singh, its form grew with the community's history, and its wording is set out in the Sikh code of conduct.

story.title: water for both sides
story.text: In the middle of a battle near Anandpur, a Sikh named Bhai Ghanaiya walks the field with a water bag, giving water to the wounded. To the wounded on both sides. Some Sikhs are furious and bring him before Guru Gobind Singh: he's helping the enemy. The Guru asks him why. I didn't see friends or enemies, he says. I saw your face in every one. The Guru sends him back out, with ointment and bandages as well.
story.source: Sikh tradition of Bhai Ghanaiya at Anandpur (early 1700s)
